stem: In a bid-price calculation, the minimum acceptable price is the one that sets the project's NPV equal to _____.
options: the CCA tax shield
the initial investment
zero
the profit margin
explanation: NPV = 0 means the project earns exactly the discount rate: it covers all costs and pays investors their required return. That is the lowest price the firm can charge without destroying value.

stem: How does the bid price based on NPV = 0 differ from the price at which accounting profit is zero?
options: The NPV price also covers the investors' required return on the capital tied up, so it is higher
The accounting price is higher because it includes depreciation
They are always identical when the tax rate is zero
The NPV price ignores the cost of equipment because it is already spent
explanation: Accounting break-even only covers expenses including depreciation; it ignores the time value of money. NPV break-even makes the PV of after-tax flows equal the investment, which requires a larger annual net revenue.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a step in finding a bid price?
options: Set NPV = 0 and compute the PV of the known flows (CAPEX, NWC, salvage, CCA shield)
Divide the remaining PV by the annuity factor to get the required after-tax annual amount
Divide by (1 - T) and add the cash costs
Divide the required after-tax annuity by the number of years N
explanation: A level annual amount that has a given present value is found by dividing by the annuity factor, not by N, because the payments occur in the future. The other three steps are the standard sequence.

stem: Why must the required after-tax annual amount be divided by (1 - T) when finding the bid price?
options: The tax rate applies only to the first year
Net revenue is taxed, so the pre-tax amount must exceed the after-tax need
(1 − T) converts a nominal flow into a real flow
The CCA shield must be added back first
explanation: The after-tax annuity equals [(P - v)Q - FC](1 - T). To recover the pre-tax figure we undo the tax by dividing by (1 - T), then add the cash costs to get total revenue.

stem: Okotoks Steel bids exactly the NPV = 0 price and wins the contract. What does that imply about the project?
options: It earns a 0% return, since its NPV is zero
It creates a positive NPV equal to the CCA tax shield
It breaks even on accounting profit but not on cash flow
It earns exactly its required return (IRR = k): no value is added or lost
explanation: At the break-even price the PV of the inflows equals the PV of the outflows at the required rate, so the IRR equals the required return. The firm is indifferent; to add value it would need a price above that level.

stem: In the bid-price equation, after-tax net revenue = [(P - v)Q - FC](1 - T). Which item is NOT inside the bracket?
options: Variable cost per unit v (a cash cost)
CCA (a non-cash deduction)
Fixed cash costs FC (a cash cost)
Price per unit P (cash revenue)
explanation: The bracket contains cash revenue and cash costs only. CCA is not a cash cost; its tax saving is counted once in the PV of CCA tax shield, so including it in the bracket would double count.

stem: If the required return rises and nothing else changes, the bid price per unit rises.
options: True
False
explanation: A higher k lowers the PV of salvage and tax shields and raises the annuity needed to repay the investment at that rate; the required after-tax net revenue grows and so does the price.

stem: To submit a bid, a firm must put land it owns at the project's disposal, with an after-tax market value of $300,000 now and $320,000 in five years. Which cash flows go into the bid calculation?
options: Nothing, because the firm already owns the land
-$300,000 at time 0 only
-$300,000 at time 0 and +$320,000 at year 5
The land's original purchase price
explanation: Land has an opportunity cost: the project gives up the after-tax sale proceeds today, and the land comes back at its after-tax value at the end. Both flows are in the NPV = 0 equation.

stem: Bow Valley Plastics will bid on a 4-year contract for 25,000 units a year. Equipment costs $620,000 (CCA rate 30%, half-year rule, sold for $70,000 at year 4, pool open). NWC of $60,000 is recovered at the end. Variable cost is $18.40 a unit, fixed cash costs $150,000 a year, T = 30%, k = 14%. What is the lowest price per unit that gives NPV = 0?

Wetaskiwin Data Services must set annual contract revenue for 3 years. Computer equipment costs $275,000 (CCA rate 45%, AII applies, worthless at the end, pool open) and $20,000 of NWC is recovered at the end. Annual cash costs are $190,000, T = 28%, k = 15%. What annual revenue gives NPV = 0?

Nechako Components bids on a 5-year contract for 30,000 units a year. Equipment costs $540,000 (CCA rate 20%, half-year rule, sold for $60,000 in year 5, pool open); NWC of $45,000 is recovered at the end. Variable cost is $22.60 a unit and fixed cash costs are $210,000 a year. T = 35%, k = 12%. What is the lowest price per unit that gives NPV = 0?

steps.label: Required after-tax net revenue per year
Required pre-tax net revenue = after-tax / (1 - T)
Required annual revenue = pre-tax + FC + v x Q

keystrokes: Compute the PV of the known flows, divide by 3.6048, divide by 0.65, add costs, divide by 30000

errors.label: Did not divide by (1 - T)
errors.explain: The annuity found is after tax. Revenue minus costs must be larger by 1/(1 - T).

errors.label: Divided the PV by N instead of the annuity factor
errors.explain: Use the annuity factor, not N.

errors.label: Left out the CCA shield
errors.explain: The shield lowers the net cost of the equipment and so lowers the price needed.

explanation: NPV = 0: PV of known pieces, then the required annuity, then un-tax, add costs and divide by quantity.

stem: Kootenay Switchgear bids on a 3-year order of 12,000 units a year. Equipment costs $350,000 (CCA rate 25%, half-year rule, sold for $40,000 at year 3, pool open); $30,000 of NWC is recovered at the end. Variable cost is $31.50 a unit, fixed cash costs $95,000 a year, T = 32%, k = 10%. Find the lowest price per unit that makes NPV = 0.

steps.label: Required after-tax net revenue per year

keystrokes: N = 3, I/Y = 10, PV = known PV, CPT PMT

errors.label: Did not divide by (1 - T)
errors.explain: Net revenue is taxed, so divide the after-tax need by (1 - T).

errors.label: Left out the fixed cash costs
errors.explain: The price must also cover FC.

explanation: Same five steps as always; the quantity is only used at the end.

stem: Fraser Valley Labels will print 50,000 packs a year for 5 years. Equipment costs $480,000 (CCA rate 30%, half-year rule, sold for $30,000 at year 5, pool open) and sits on land the firm owns, worth $300,000 after tax now and $320,000 after tax in 5 years. NWC of $40,000 is recovered at the end. Variable cost is $2.70 a pack, fixed cash costs $160,000, T = 34%, k = 12%. What is the lowest price per pack for NPV = 0?

steps.label: Required after-tax net revenue per year

keystrokes: Compute the known PV with land in and out, then CPT PMT with N = 5, I/Y = 12

errors.label: Left out the land's opportunity cost and return
errors.explain: The land has an opportunity cost: the firm gives up its after-tax sale value now and gets it back later.

errors.label: Did not divide by (1 - T)
errors.explain: Divide the after-tax requirement by (1 - T).

errors.label: Left out the CCA shield
errors.explain: The CCA shield reduces the price needed.

explanation: Land goes in at its after-tax opportunity value both ways; the rest of the five steps are unchanged.

stem: Nechako Components (equipment $540,000, CCA rate 20%, half-year rule, sold for $60,000 at year 5, pool open; NWC $45,000; 30,000 units a year; variable cost $22.60; fixed cash costs $210,000; T = 35%; k = 12%) wants its 5-year contract to add $75,000 of NPV instead of zero. What price per unit does it need?
solution: Set NPV = 75,000: PV of operations must equal 75,000 - known PV = 75,000 + 421,070.78 = 496,070.78
keystrokes: Same steps as the zero-NPV bid with 75,000 added to the PV that operations must supply

errors.label: Subtracted the target NPV instead of adding it
errors.explain: A positive target NPV means operations must generate more PV, so the price rises.

errors.label: Did not divide by (1 - T)
errors.explain: Divide by (1 - T).

explanation: A required NPV simply raises the PV that the operating annuity must supply.

stem: Nechako Components (equipment $540,000, CCA rate 20%, half-year rule, sold for $60,000 at year 5, pool open; NWC $45,000; variable cost $22.60; fixed cash costs $210,000; T = 35%; k = 12%) can sell its product at $38.50. How many units a year must it sell for NPV = 0? Answer in units, to the nearest unit.
solution: (P - v)Q - FC = pre-tax net revenue, so Q = (pre-tax + FC)/(P - v)
keystrokes: Compute the pre-tax requirement, add 210000, divide by 15.9

errors.label: Did not divide by (1 - T)
errors.explain: Net revenue is taxed: divide by (1 - T) first.

errors.label: Left out the fixed cash costs
errors.explain: Fixed costs must be covered before profit.

explanation: Same NPV = 0 requirement, solved for quantity instead of price.

stem: Cascade Rail owns an old locomotive, the last asset in its CCA class, that earns nothing more. It is deciding whether to sell it at the end of year 5 or keep it and keep claiming CCA. What is the opportunity cost of selling at year 5?
options: The present value of the CCA tax shields it gives up on the remaining UCC
The original purchase price of the locomotive
The CCA already claimed in years 1 to 5
The recapture tax that would be due on the sale
explanation: Selling ends the CCA stream. At year 5 that stream is worth UCC x d x T/(k + d). Past CCA is history, and recapture tax is already inside the after-tax sale proceeds.

stem: Clean Air Industries owns land it could use for a new sensor line. Which three choices should it compare?
options: Build the project, sell the project, or abandon the project
Sell the land now and buy equivalent land back later; keep renting it out; use it for the new project
Sell the land, keep the land idle, or give the land away
Use the land now, use the land in a year, or use the land in two years
explanation: The land has alternative uses and each is a different set of cash flows. The lecture compares the two existing uses first (sell and rebuy versus rent) and then tests the winner against the project.

stem: When comparing a sale at year N with continuing to hold the asset, the sale gives up the present value of the remaining CCA _____.
options: recapture
terminal loss
capital gain
tax shield
explanation: Continuing to hold keeps the declining stream of CCA deductions going. Their tax saving, T x CCA, is the shield the sale gives up, valued as a declining perpetuity.

stem: How do the cash flows from selling at year N differ from the cash flows from holding the asset?
options: Selling brings after-tax cash now but ends the CCA shield; holding keeps the shield
Selling gives the CCA shield now; holding gives the proceeds
Selling is taxed; holding is not taxed at all
Selling and holding give the same cash flows except for timing
explanation: Selling swaps a lump of after-tax cash (POD less tax on recapture or plus the terminal-loss refund) for the loss of all later CCA shields. Holding does the opposite.

stem: When valuing 'sell at year 5 versus hold', which of the following should NOT enter the analysis?
options: The after-tax proceeds from the sale
The tax effect (recapture or terminal loss) of the sale
The original purchase price of the asset
The CCA tax shields that would continue if the asset is held
explanation: The purchase price is a sunk cost. Only what changes between selling and holding matters: the proceeds, their tax effect and the lost future shields.

stem: Why can a firm be better off selling an asset at year N even though the sale ends its CCA deductions?
options: CCA deductions are no longer tax deductible after year N
The sale proceeds are never taxed when an asset is sold
Cash from the sale arrives now; the lost shields arrive slowly and shrink
UCC always exceeds the sale price, creating a tax refund
explanation: The lost shield is worth UCC x d x T/(k + d), a fraction of UCC. The sale delivers POD plus a tax effect immediately. Without other benefits from holding, selling usually wins.

stem: A sell-versus-hold analysis at year 4 gives an NPV of +$31,005 for selling. What does this mean?
options: Selling beats holding by $31,005 in year-4 dollars
Holding the asset adds $31,005 of value
The asset's sale price at year 4 is $31,005
The asset will produce $31,005 of profit before tax
explanation: The NPV compares the two strategies at a common date: after-tax proceeds less the PV of the shield lost. A positive value favours the sale.

stem: Which sequence correctly compares the three choices for the land in the Clean Air example?
options: Compare all three using each choice's accounting profit
Evaluate the project alone and ignore the land
Discount all three choices at different rates and pick the largest cash flow
Compare 'rent' with 'sell and buy back', then the winner with 'use for the project'
explanation: Each comparison uses incremental NPV. The rent-versus-sell step shows what the land is worth in its best alternative use, which is the opportunity cost charged to the project.

stem: Other things equal, a higher discount rate makes selling the asset at year N more attractive relative to holding it.
options: True
False
explanation: The lost shield is UCC x d x T/(k + d); a higher k reduces it, while the sale proceeds do not depend on k. The comparison tilts further towards selling.

stem: Foothills Rail will sell its last idle crane at the end of year 5 for $24,000 and close the class. The crane cost $40,000, its UCC after year 5 CCA is $18,400, CCA rate 30%, T = 36% and k = 10%. If it keeps the crane it keeps claiming CCA on the UCC. What is the NPV, at year 5, of selling instead of holding?
explanation: After-tax proceeds = 24,000 - 0.36 x (24,000 - 18,400) = 21,984.00. Lost shield = 18,400 x 0.30 x 0.36/(0.10 + 0.30) = 4,968.00. NPV = 21,984.00 - 4,968.00 = $17,016.00. Ignoring the lost shield overstates the gain; adding it instead of subtracting is a sign error.

stem: An idle machine (CCA rate 20%) has a UCC of $33,177.60 after year 4 CCA. T = 35% and k = 12%. What is the value at year 4 of the CCA tax shields the firm gives up if it sells the machine, closing the class?
explanation: Value of the declining shield stream = UCC x d x T/(k + d) = 33,177.60 x 0.20 x 0.35/0.32 = $7,257.60 at year 4. Using k - d gives a nonsensical value; omitting T or the (k + d) divisor gives other wrong answers.

stem: Bow Valley Aggregates owns an idle machine bought for $72,000 (CCA rate 20%, half-year rule). At the end of year 4, after claiming year 4 CCA, it can sell it for $41,000, closing the class, or keep it and keep claiming CCA. T = 35% and k = 12%. What is the NPV at year 4 of selling instead of holding?

steps.label: PV at year 4 of the shield given up

keystrokes: Compute UCC; CF_AT = 41000 - 0.35(41000 - UCC); lost shield = UCC x 0.2 x 0.35 / 0.32; subtract

errors.label: Ignored the shield given up
errors.explain: Selling ends the CCA stream; its PV is the opportunity cost of selling.

errors.label: Taxed the whole proceeds
errors.explain: Tax is only on POD - UCC (recapture).

errors.label: Used k - d in the lost-shield denominator
errors.explain: The shield declines at d, so the discount denominator is k + d.

explanation: Net the after-tax cash from selling against the PV of the shield you would otherwise keep.

stem: Prairie Pallet has an idle machine bought for $50,000 (CCA rate 30%, half-year rule, T = 30%, k = 10%). It will be sold either at the end of year 3 for $22,000 or at the end of year 4 for $17,500; either sale (after that year's CCA) closes the class and the machine earns nothing meanwhile. How much more is the present value today of selling at year 3 than selling at year 4? Count the CCA tax shields and the tax effect of the sale.

steps.label: PV today if sold at year 3
PV today if sold at year 4

solution: Sale at year 3: recapture 1,175.00, CF_AT = 21,647.50. Sale at year 4: recapture 2,922.50, CF_AT = 16,623.25
PV (year 4 sale) = shields years 1-3 + (year-4 shield 1,874.25 + CF_AT 16,623.25)/1.1^4 = 19,852.30
keystrokes: CF0 = 0, C01 = 2250, C02 = 3825, C03 = 2677.5 + 21647.5, NPV I = 10 for the year-3 plan; extend to C04 for the year-4 plan

errors.label: Compared only the after-tax sale proceeds discounted
errors.explain: Waiting a year also earns one more year of CCA shield; both plans must count all shields.

errors.label: Did not discount the year-4 flows by four years
errors.explain: Year-4 flows are discounted four years.

explanation: Compare the PV of the two complete plans: shields plus after-tax sale in each.

stem: Okotoks Industrial owns land worth $2,500,000 after tax today, rented for $260,000 a year (taxed at 25%) for the next 5 years. It could instead sell the land now and buy equivalent land back in 5 years for $2,500,000 (the market is flat). The discount rate is 12%. What is the NPV of renting minus selling and buying back? A negative answer means selling is better.

steps.label: PV of the land at year 5
NPV of renting vs selling and rebuying

solution: Renting means giving up the sale proceeds now (-2,500,000) and keeping the land worth 2,500,000 in year 5
NPV = -$378,501.50; negative, so selling and buying back is better
keystrokes: N = 5, I/Y = 12, PMT = 195000, CPT PV; FV = 2500000, CPT PV; subtract 2500000

errors.label: Used the rent before tax
errors.explain: Rent is income and is taxed at 25%.

errors.label: Did not discount the land at year 5
errors.explain: The land is bought back in 5 years; discount it.

errors.label: Reversed the sign (selling minus renting)
errors.explain: The question asks for rent minus sell; the sign tells which is better.

explanation: The lecture's first comparison: renting out versus selling and buying back the land.

stem: Bow Valley Dairy can sell a machine from an open pool (other assets remain) for $35,000 at the end of year 3. The sale has no immediate tax effect, but it removes the proceeds from the pool's UCC. CCA rate 20%, T = 35%, k = 10%. What is the NPV at year 3 of selling instead of holding, counting the shield lost on the amount sold?

steps.label: PV at year 3 of the shield lost

errors.label: Ignored the lost shield
errors.explain: Selling shrinks the pool, so the CCA on that amount is given up.

errors.label: Used k - d
errors.explain: The denominator is k + d.

explanation: An open-pool sale is received untaxed but costs the shield on the amount sold.

stem: Fraser Rentals must choose between two vans, one lasting 3 years and one lasting 5 years. Each will be replaced by an identical van when it wears out, and both provide the same service. Which method compares them properly?
options: Compare the NPVs of costs directly
Equivalent annual cost over each van's own life
Compare the IRRs of the two vans
Compare the payback periods of the two vans
explanation: The vans have unequal lives and a continuing need, so each needs to be turned into a cost per year. EAC = PV of costs divided by the annuity factor for the van's own life.

stem: The equivalent annual cost of an asset is its present value of costs divided by the _____ factor for its life.
options: perpetuity
discount
growth
annuity
explanation: The EAC is the level annual payment with the same PV as the costs over the asset's life, so it is PV/[(1 - 1/(1 + k)^N)/k].

stem: Why can comparing the raw present values of costs of a 3-year machine and a 5-year machine give the wrong answer?
options: The raw PV ignores the CCA tax shield
The shorter-lived machine's smaller PV buys fewer years of service
Raw PVs are stated in different currencies
The longer-lived machine always has the lower PV of costs
explanation: Raw PVs are totals over different time spans. A 3-year machine will look cheaper even if its annual cost is higher. EAC puts them on a per-year footing.
